questions.question: Let $f(x)=\int x^3\sqrt{3-x^2}\,dx$. If $5f(\sqrt2)=-4$, then $f(1)$ is equal to:
questions.key_idea: Put $3-x^2=t^2$ so that $x\,dx=-t\,dt$ and $x^2=3-t^2$ turns the integrand into a polynomial in $t$.

alternate_solutions.idea: Avoid the constant: write $f(1)=f(\sqrt2)+\int_{\sqrt2}^{1}x^3\sqrt{3-x^2}\,dx$ and evaluate the definite integral with $u=3-x^2$.

useful_results: $\int x^{2k+1}\,g(x^2)\,dx$: put $u=x^2$ (or $u=\sqrt{a-x^2}$ when a root is present); odd powers of $x$ always supply the $du$.
In general $\int x^3\sqrt{a-x^2}\,dx=\frac{(a-x^2)^{5/2}}{5}-\frac{a\,(a-x^2)^{3/2}}{3}+C$; for $a=3$ this is the antiderivative found above.
A condition such as $f(x_0)=k$ fixes the constant $C$ only after you have a closed-form antiderivative; a definite integral from $x_0$ avoids $C$ altogether.

questions.question: If $\int e^{x}\left(\frac{x\sin^{-1}x}{\sqrt{1-x^2}}+\frac{\sin^{-1}x}{(1-x^2)^{3/2}}+\frac{x}{1-x^2}\right)dx=g(x)+C$, where $C$ is the constant of integration, then $g\left(\frac12\right)$ equals:
questions.key_idea: Recognise the bracket as $f(x)+f'(x)$ with $f(x)=\frac{x\sin^{-1}x}{\sqrt{1-x^2}}$, so the integral is $e^xf(x)$.
solution: Let $f(x)=\frac{x\sin^{-1}x}{\sqrt{1-x^2}}$. Then $f'(x)=\frac{\sin^{-1}x}{(1-x^2)^{3/2}}+\frac{x}{1-x^2}$, so the bracket is $f(x)+f'(x)$.
useful_results: $\int e^{x}\{f(x)+f'(x)\}dx=e^xf(x)+C$ (reverse of the product rule). Also $\int e^{ax}\{af(x)+f'(x)\}dx=e^{ax}f(x)+C$.
Recognition cue: after removing $e^x$, the bracket splits into a 'function' part and its derivative; look for the part with the most complicated factor (here $\sin^{-1}x$) and differentiate it.
Derivative used: $\frac{d}{dx}\frac{x}{\sqrt{1-x^2}}=\frac{1}{(1-x^2)^{3/2}}$, and $\frac{d}{dx}\sin^{-1}x=\frac1{\sqrt{1-x^2}}$.
Check on this question: at $x=0$ the bracket is $0$, and $\frac{d}{dx}\left[e^xf(x)\right]_{x=0}=f(0)+f'(0)=0$, consistent.

concepts: Integration by substitution (Möbius-type) with fractional powers
questions.question: Let $I(x)=\int\frac{dx}{(x-11)^{11/13}(x+15)^{15/13}}$. If $I(37)-I(24)=\frac14\left(\frac{1}{b^{1/13}}-\frac{1}{c^{1/13}}\right)$, $b,c\in\mathbb N$, then $3(b+c)$ is equal to:
questions.key_idea: The exponents add to $2$, so factor out $(x+15)^2$ and substitute $t=\frac{x-11}{x+15}$, whose differential is $\frac{26\,dx}{(x+15)^2}$.
useful_results: $\int\frac{dx}{(x-a)^{m}(x-b)^{n}}$ with $m+n=2$, $m\neq1$: put $t=\frac{x-a}{x-b}$; then $dt=\frac{(a-b)\,dx}{(x-b)^2}$ and the integral is $\frac{1}{(a-b)(1-m)}\left(\frac{x-a}{x-b}\right)^{1-m}+C$.
For $m=1$ (so $n=1$) the same substitution gives $\frac1{a-b}\ln\left|\frac{x-a}{x-b}\right|+C$.
Recognition cue: two linear factors raised to fractional powers whose exponents sum to $2$ (or the form $\frac{1}{(x-a)^{k}(x-b)^{2-k}}$).
Check here: $m=\frac{11}{13}$, $a-b=26$, so coefficient $\frac{1}{26\cdot 2/13}=\frac14$, as found.

questions.question: Let $\int x^3\sin x\,dx=g(x)+C$, where $C$ is the constant of integration. If $8\left(g\left(\frac\pi2\right)+g'\left(\frac\pi2\right)\right)=\alpha\pi^3+\beta\pi^2+\gamma$, $\alpha,\beta,\gamma\in\mathbb Z$, then $\alpha+\beta-\gamma$ equals:
questions.key_idea: Repeated integration by parts (tabular method) for polynomial $\times$ trigonometric, and $g'(x)=x^3\sin x$ directly.
solution: Tabular method for $\int x^3\sin x\,dx$: derivatives of $x^3$ are $3x^2,\,6x,\,6,\,0$; integrals of $\sin x$ are $-\cos x,\,-\sin x,\,\cos x,\,\sin x$ with alternating signs $+,-,+,-$.

alternate_solutions.idea: Take the imaginary part of $\int x^3e^{ix}\,dx$, which needs only the formula $\int x^ne^{ax}dx=e^{ax}\sum(-1)^k\frac{n!}{(n-k)!}\frac{x^{n-k}}{a^{k+1}}$.
solution: The imaginary part gives $\int x^3\sin x\,dx=(3x^2-6)\sin x+(6x-x^3)\cos x+C$, the same $g(x)$.
At $\frac\pi2$ this is $\frac{3\pi^2}{4}-6$, and $g'\left(\frac\pi2\right)=\frac{\pi^3}{8}$, so $8(g+g')=\pi^3+6\pi^2-48$ and $\alpha+\beta-\gamma=55$. Same answer.

useful_results: Tabular (DI) method: for $\int P(x)\,\{\sin x\ \text{or}\ \cos x\ \text{or}\ e^{ax}\}dx$ with polynomial $P$, differentiate $P$ down to $0$, integrate the other factor repeatedly, pair diagonally with signs $+,-,+,\dots$.
$\int P(x)e^{ax}dx=e^{ax}\left(\frac{P}{a}-\frac{P'}{a^2}+\frac{P''}{a^3}-\cdots\right)$; put $a=i$ and take real/imaginary part for $\cos$/$\sin$.
Never integrate to evaluate $g'$: if $\int h=g+C$, then $g'=h$. Here $g'\left(\frac\pi2\right)=\left(\frac\pi2\right)^3\cdot1$.
Numerical check: at $x=\frac\pi2$, $g=\frac{3\pi^2}{4}-6\approx1.2$; $8(g+g')\approx42.22=\pi^3+6\pi^2-48$.

questions.question: If $f(x)=\int\frac{1}{x^{1/4}\left(1+x^{1/4}\right)}dx$, $f(0)=-6$, then $f(1)$ is equal to:
questions.key_idea: Put $x^{1/4}=t$: then $dx=4t^3dt$ and the integrand becomes the rational function $\frac{4t^2}{1+t}$.

alternate_solutions.idea: Substitute $u=1+x^{1/4}$ and use a definite integral from $x=0$ to $x=1$, so the constant $C$ never appears.

useful_results: $\int R\left(x^{p/q}\right)dx$: put $x=t^q$ (the lcm of the denominators of the exponents) to reach a rational function in $t$.
$\frac{t^2}{1+t}=t-1+\frac{1}{1+t}$ (divide first when the numerator degree is at least the denominator's).
The condition $f(0)=-6$ is used as $x\to0^+$: then $x^{1/4}\to0$ and $\ln(1+0)=0$, which fixes $C=-6$.
Check: $f'(x)=x^{-1/2}-x^{-3/4}+\frac{x^{-3/4}}{1+x^{1/4}}$; at $x=1$ this is $1-1+\frac12=\frac12$, the value of the integrand at $x=1$.

questions.question: If $\int\frac{1}{a^2\sin^2x+b^2\cos^2x}dx=\frac1{12}\tan^{-1}(3\tan x)+\text{constant}$, then the maximum value of $a\sin x+b\cos x$ is:
questions.key_idea: Divide by $\cos^2x$ and put $\tan x=t$ to compare with $\frac1{12}\tan^{-1}(3t)$; the maximum of $a\sin x+b\cos x$ is $\sqrt{a^2+b^2}$.
solution: Then $a=6$, $b=2$ (the pair $a=-6,b=-2$ gives the same maximum).
The maximum value of $a\sin x+b\cos x$ is $\sqrt{a^2+b^2}=\sqrt{36+4}=\sqrt{40}$.

alternate_solutions.idea: Differentiate the given antiderivative: the integrand must equal its derivative, which reads off $a^2$ and $b^2$ directly.
solution: Hence $a^2=36$ and $b^2=4$ (compare the values at $x=0$ and $x=\frac\pi2$).
Maximum of $a\sin x+b\cos x$ is $\sqrt{a^2+b^2}=\sqrt{40}$; no need to fix the signs of $a,b$. Same answer.

useful_results: $\int\frac{dx}{a^2\sin^2x+b^2\cos^2x}=\frac1{ab}\tan^{-1}\left(\frac ab\tan x\right)+C$ for $ab>0$ (divide by $\cos^2x$).
Only $a^2$ and $b^2$ appear in the integrand, so the question determines $\sqrt{a^2+b^2}$ uniquely even though the signs of $a,b$ are free.
$\max(a\sin x+b\cos x)=\sqrt{a^2+b^2}$, $\min=-\sqrt{a^2+b^2}$ (write it as $R\sin(x+\phi)$).
Similarly $\int\frac{dx}{a+b\sin^2x}$ and $\int\frac{dx}{a+b\cos^2x}$ use the same $\tan x=t$ substitution.

questions.question: Let $I(x)=\int\frac{6}{\sin^2x(1-\cot x)^2}dx$. If $I(0)=3$, then $I\left(\frac\pi{12}\right)$ is equal to:
questions.key_idea: Write $\sin^2x(1-\cot x)^2=(\sin x-\cos x)^2$, divide by $\cos^2x$ and put $\tan x=t$ to get $\int\frac{6\,dt}{(t-1)^2}$.

alternate_solutions.idea: Use $\csc^2x\,dx=-d(\cot x)$ directly: put $u=1-\cot x$, so no division by $\cos^2x$ is needed (the condition $I(0)=3$ is used as a limit).
solution: As $x\to0^+$, $\cot x\to\infty$ so $-\frac{6}{1-\cot x}\to0$; hence $I(0)=3$ gives $C=3$.

useful_results: $\csc^2x\,dx=-d(\cot x)$ and $\sec^2x\,dx=d(\tan x)$: if the integrand is a function of $\cot x$ (or $\tan x$) times $\csc^2x$ (or $\sec^2x$), substitute at once.
Two antiderivatives of the same function differ by a constant: here $-\frac6{1-\cot x}=-\frac{6}{\tan x-1}-6$, which is why the constants $3$ and $-3$ differ.
$\tan\frac\pi{12}=2-\sqrt3$, $\cot\frac\pi{12}=2+\sqrt3$; $\tan\frac{5\pi}{12}=2+\sqrt3$.

concepts: Integration of $\frac{a\cos x+b\sin x}{c\cos x+d\sin x}$ by the derivative method
questions.question: Let $\int\frac{2-\tan x}{3+\tan x}dx=\frac12\left(\alpha x+\log_e|\beta\sin x+\gamma\cos x|\right)+C$, where $C$ is the constant of integration. Then $\alpha+\frac\gamma\beta$ is equal to:
questions.key_idea: Convert to $\frac{2\cos x-\sin x}{3\cos x+\sin x}$ and write the numerator as $a\,(\text{denominator})'+b\,(\text{denominator})$.
solution: $\int\frac{2-\tan x}{3+\tan x}dx=\int\frac{2\cos x-\sin x}{3\cos x+\sin x}dx$.
Write $2\cos x-\sin x=a(-3\sin x+\cos x)+b(3\cos x+\sin x)$, where $-3\sin x+\cos x$ is the derivative of the denominator.
Comparing the coefficients of $\cos x$ and $\sin x$: $a+3b=2$ ... (i) and $-3a+b=-1$ ... (ii).
$I=\frac12\int\frac{-3\sin x+\cos x}{3\cos x+\sin x}dx+\frac12\int dx=\frac12\ln|3\cos x+\sin x|+\frac12x$.
$\alpha+\frac\gamma\beta=1+\frac31=4$. (The key (D) $7$ does not match this; the printed options (C) and (D) are both $7$, so the option list is faulty.)
questions.correction_note: The PDF's working gives alpha=1, beta=1, gamma=3 and alpha+gamma/beta=4, which is correct, but its answer key says D (=7), which is wrong; options C and D are both printed as 7 and none equals 4. Kept 4 as the answer and flagged the key. Scaling beta, gamma by a common factor only changes the constant, so gamma/beta=3 is forced.

alternate_solutions.idea: Put $t=\tan x$ and use partial fractions in $t$: $\frac{2-t}{(3+t)(1+t^2)}$.
solution: Put $t=-3$: $5=10A$, so $A=\frac12$. Coefficient of $t^2$: $0=A+B$, so $B=-\frac12$. Constant term: $2=A+3C$, so $C=\frac12$. (Check, coefficient of $t$: $-1=3B+C=-1$.)
With $t=\tan x$: $\frac12\ln|3+\tan x|+\frac12\ln|\cos x|+\frac x2=\frac12\left(x+\ln|3\cos x+\sin x|\right)$ (since $-\frac14\ln\sec^2x=\frac12\ln|\cos x|$).

useful_results: $\int\frac{a\cos x+b\sin x}{c\cos x+d\sin x}dx$: write numerator $=A\,(c\cos x+d\sin x)'+B\,(c\cos x+d\sin x)$; then the integral is $A\ln|c\cos x+d\sin x|+Bx+C$.
For $\int\frac{p\sin x+q\cos x+r}{\ldots}$ with a constant added, the numerator takes a third term $C$ and one more standard integral $\int\frac{dx}{c\cos x+d\sin x}$ remains.
Only the ratio $\gamma:\beta$ is determined by such an identity: multiplying $\beta,\gamma$ by $k>0$ adds $\frac12\ln k$ to the constant.
Check: derivative of $\frac12\left(x+\ln(\sin x+3\cos x)\right)$ at $x=0$ is $\frac12\left(1+\frac13\right)=\frac23$, and $\frac{2-0}{3+0}=\frac23$.

concepts: Integration by substitution (inverse trigonometric function of $x^3+x^{-3}$)
questions.question: The integral $\int\frac{\left(x^8-x^2\right)dx}{\left(x^{12}+3x^6+1\right)\tan^{-1}\left(x^3+\frac1{x^3}\right)}$ is equal to:
questions.key_idea: Put $t=\tan^{-1}\left(x^3+x^{-3}\right)$; then $dt$ reproduces $\frac{3(x^8-x^2)}{x^{12}+3x^6+1}dx$ and the integral is $\frac13\int\frac{dt}t$.
useful_results: Form $\int\frac{f'(x)}{f(x)}dx=\ln|f(x)|+C$ with $f=\tan^{-1}u$: the derivative $f'=\frac{u'}{1+u^2}$ is the other factor to spot.
For $u=x^n+x^{-n}$: $1+u^2=x^{2n}+3+x^{-2n}$ and $u'=n(x^{n-1}-x^{-n-1})$; multiply through by $x^{2n}$ to get $x^{4n}+3x^{2n}+1$.
Recognition cue: a polynomial of the shape $x^{12}+3x^6+1$ (palindromic) hints at dividing by $x^6$ and putting $x^3\pm x^{-3}=w$.

questions.question: For $x\in\left(-\frac\pi2,\frac\pi2\right)$, if $y(x)=\int\frac{\csc x+\sin x}{\csc x\sec x+\tan x\sin^2x}dx$, and $\lim_{x\to\left(\frac\pi2\right)^-}y(x)=0$, then $y\left(\frac\pi4\right)$ is equal to:
questions.key_idea: After simplifying to $\frac{(1+\sin^2x)\cos x}{1+\sin^4x}$, put $\sin x=t$ and divide by $t^2$: $\int\frac{1+t^{-2}}{t^2+t^{-2}}dt$ with $u=t-\frac1t$.
solution: Write numerator and denominator over $\sin x$ and $\sin x\cos x$: $\csc x+\sin x=\frac{1+\sin^2x}{\sin x}$; $\csc x\sec x+\tan x\sin^2x=\frac{1+\sin^4x}{\sin x\cos x}$.
As $x\to\frac\pi2$, $\sin x\to1$ so $u\to0$ and $y\to c$; hence $c=0$.
questions.correction_note: PDF labels the antiderivative f(x) and writes f'(pi/2)=0, f'(pi/4); these should be y(x) with limit y(x) -> 0 as x -> pi/2 and y(pi/4). Notation only; the working and answer (B) are right.

alternate_solutions.idea: Factor $1+t^4=(t^2+\sqrt2t+1)(t^2-\sqrt2t+1)$ and split $\frac{1+t^2}{1+t^4}$ into two arctangent integrals.
solution: $\frac{1+t^2}{1+t^4}=\frac12\left[\frac1{t^2+\sqrt2t+1}+\frac1{t^2-\sqrt2t+1}\right]$ (add the two fractions to check: numerator $2(t^2+1)$).
At $t=1$: $(\sqrt2+1)(\sqrt2-1)=1$, so the two angles add to $\frac\pi2$; the limit condition gives $0=\frac1{\sqrt2}\cdot\frac\pi2+c$, so $c=-\frac{\pi}{2\sqrt2}$.

useful_results: $\int\frac{1+t^2}{1+t^4}dt=\frac1{\sqrt2}\tan^{-1}\frac{t^2-1}{\sqrt2\,t}+C$ and $\int\frac{1-t^2}{1+t^4}dt=\frac1{2\sqrt2}\ln\left|\frac{t^2+\sqrt2t+1}{t^2-\sqrt2t+1}\right|+C$ (divide by $t^2$ and use $t-\frac1t$ or $t+\frac1t$).
Rule: $\frac{1+t^{-2}}{\ldots}$ pairs with $u=t-\frac1t$ ($du=(1+t^{-2})dt$, $t^2+t^{-2}=u^2+2$); $\frac{1-t^{-2}}{\ldots}$ pairs with $u=t+\frac1t$ ($t^2+t^{-2}=u^2-2$).
$1+t^4=(t^2+\sqrt2t+1)(t^2-\sqrt2t+1)$ (Sophie Germain-type factorisation of $a^4+4b^4$ with $b^4=\frac14$).
A limit condition such as $y\to0$ at an end point of the domain fixes $C$ when the integrand is not defined there.

questions.question: If $\int\frac{\sin^{3/2}x+\cos^{3/2}x}{\sqrt{\sin^3x\cos^3x\sin(x-\theta)}}dx=A\sqrt{\cos\theta\tan x-\sin\theta}+B\sqrt{\cos\theta-\sin\theta\cot x}+C$, where $C$ is the integration constant, then $AB$ is equal to:
questions.key_idea: Split the numerator; each part becomes $\frac{\sec^2x\,dx}{\sqrt{\tan x\cos\theta-\sin\theta}}$ or the cosecant analogue, because $\sec x\sin(x-\theta)=\cos\theta\tan x-\sin\theta$.
solution: Now $\sec x\sin(x-\theta)=\tan x\cos\theta-\sin\theta$ and $\csc x\sin(x-\theta)=\cos\theta-\cot x\sin\theta$, so $I=I_1+I_2$ with $I_1=\int\frac{\sec^2x\,dx}{\sqrt{\tan x\cos\theta-\sin\theta}}$.
Comparing with the given form: $A=\frac2{\cos\theta}$ and $B=\frac2{\sin\theta}$.
questions.correction_note: PDF writes I1 = (2/cos theta) sqrt(tan x cot theta - sin theta); the radicand must be tan x cos theta - sin theta (cos, not cot). Later working and answer (D) are right.
useful_results: Two-term integrands with $\sin^{3/2}$, $\cos^{3/2}$ over $\sqrt{\sin^3x\cos^3x\,\cdot}$: divide by $\sin^{3/2}x\cos^{3/2}x$ to get $\sec^{3/2}x$ and $\csc^{3/2}x$, then write each as $\frac{\sec^2x}{\sqrt{\sec x\,(\cdot)}}$.
$\sin(x-\theta)=\sin x\cos\theta-\cos x\sin\theta$, hence $\frac{\sin(x-\theta)}{\cos x}=\tan x\cos\theta-\sin\theta$ and $\frac{\sin(x-\theta)}{\sin x}=\cos\theta-\cot x\sin\theta$.
$\int\frac{f'(x)\,dx}{\sqrt{f(x)}}=2\sqrt{f(x)}+C$; with $f=\tan x\cos\theta-\sin\theta$, $f'=\cos\theta\sec^2x$ giving the factor $\frac2{\cos\theta}$.

concepts: Integration by parts (derivative of a quotient)
questions.question: Let $I(x)=\int\frac{x^2\left(x\sec^2x+\tan x\right)}{(x\tan x+1)^2}dx$. If $I(0)=0$, then $I\left(\frac\pi4\right)$ is equal to:
questions.key_idea: $x\sec^2x+\tan x=(x\tan x+1)'$, so integrate $x^2\cdot\frac{w'}{w^2}$ by parts with $w=x\tan x+1$.
solution: Let $w=x\tan x+1$; then $w'=x\sec^2x+\tan x$ and the integrand is $x^2\cdot\frac{w'}{w^2}$.
Let $x\sin x+\cos x=t$; then $dt=(x\cos x+\sin x-\sin x)dx=x\cos x\,dx$.
questions.correction_note: PDF's evaluation line reads -pi/((pi/4)(1)+1), i.e. numerator pi instead of x^2 = pi^2/16, and -x^2/(x tan x+1) at pi/4 is -pi^2/(4(pi+4)). The PDF's final line has the right value. Also the PDF splits the integrand without saying it is x^2 w'/w^2; the by-parts step was written out. Answer (B) unchanged.
useful_results: $\frac{d}{dx}\left(\frac{g}{w}\right)=\frac{g'w-gw'}{w^2}$: when the numerator contains $w'$ times a simple factor $g$, integrate by parts: $\int g\frac{w'}{w^2}=-\frac gw+\int\frac{g'}{w}$.
$\frac{d}{dx}(x\tan x+1)=x\sec^2x+\tan x$ and $\frac{d}{dx}(x\sin x+\cos x)=x\cos x$: both are standard 'x times trig' derivatives worth remembering.
Pattern: $\int\frac{x\cos x}{x\sin x+\cos x}dx=\ln|x\sin x+\cos x|+C$ (numerator is the derivative of the denominator).
Numerical check: $\frac{(\pi+4)^2}{32}\approx1.5935$, $\ln1.5935\approx0.4661$; $\frac{\pi^2}{4(\pi+4)}\approx0.3455$; difference $\approx0.1206=I\left(\frac\pi4\right)$.

questions.question: If $I(x)=\int e^{\sin^2x}(\cos x\sin2x-\sin x)\,dx$ and $I(0)=1$, then $I\left(\frac\pi3\right)$ is equal to:
questions.key_idea: With $f=\sin^2x$ and $g=\cos x$: $f'g+g'=\cos x\sin2x-\sin x$, so the integrand is $\frac{d}{dx}\left(e^{f}g\right)$.
solution: Take $f(x)=\sin^2x$, so $f'(x)=\sin2x$, and $g(x)=\cos x$, so $g'(x)=-\sin x$.
Then $g'+f'g=-\sin x+\sin2x\cos x$, exactly the bracket.

alternate_solutions.idea: Substitute $u=\cos x$: the integrand becomes $e^{1-u^2}(1-2u^2)\,du$, which is $\frac{d}{du}\left(u\,e^{1-u^2}\right)$.
solution: $\cos x\sin2x-\sin x=\sin x\,(2\cos^2x-1)$, so $I=\int e^{\sin^2x}\sin x\,(2\cos^2x-1)\,dx$.

useful_results: $\frac{d}{dx}\left(e^{f}g\right)=e^{f}\left(g'+f'g\right)$: recognise integrands of the shape $e^{f}\times(\text{sum of } g' \text{ and } f'g)$.
Special case $g=1$: $\int f'e^{f}dx=e^{f}+C$; special case $f=x$: $\int e^x(g+g')dx=e^xg+C$.
Integrals like $\int e^{-u^2}(1-2u^2)du=ue^{-u^2}+C$ close in elementary form even though $\int e^{-u^2}du$ does not.
Numerical check: $\int_0^{\pi/3}e^{\sin^2x}(\cos x\sin2x-\sin x)dx\approx0.0585=\frac12e^{3/4}-1$.

questions.question: For $\alpha,\beta,\gamma,\delta\in\mathbb N$, if $\int\left(\left(\frac xe\right)^{2x}+\left(\frac ex\right)^{2x}\right)\log_ex\,dx=\frac1\alpha\left(\frac xe\right)^{\beta x}-\frac1\gamma\left(\frac ex\right)^{\delta x}+C$, where $e=\sum_{n=0}^\infty\frac1{n!}$ and $C$ is the constant of integration, then $\alpha+2\beta+3\gamma-4\delta$ is equal to:
questions.key_idea: With $t=\left(\frac xe\right)^{2x}$, $\ln t=2x(\ln x-1)$ and $\frac{dt}{t}=2\ln x\,dx$, which supplies the $\log_ex\,dx$.
solution: Let $\left(\frac xe\right)^{2x}=t$. Taking logarithms: $\ln t=2x(\ln x-1)$.
useful_results: $\frac{d}{dx}\left(\frac xe\right)^{x}=\left(\frac xe\right)^{x}\ln x$ (since $\frac{d}{dx}\,x(\ln x-1)=\ln x$): the pair $x^x e^{-x}$ and $\ln x$ is the standard hidden derivative.
General: $\frac{d}{dx}\left(\frac xe\right)^{kx}=k\ln x\left(\frac xe\right)^{kx}$; so $\int\left(\frac xe\right)^{kx}\ln x\,dx=\frac1k\left(\frac xe\right)^{kx}+C$.
For sums $t+\frac1t$ with $dt=t\cdot(\ldots)$, after dividing you get $\int(1+t^{-2})dt=t-t^{-1}$.
Check on this question: $\frac{d}{dx}\frac12\left[\left(\frac xe\right)^{2x}-\left(\frac ex\right)^{2x}\right]$ at $x=e$ is $\frac12(2+2)\cdot1=2=(1+1)\ln e$.

questions.question: If $\int\frac{\left(\sqrt{1+x^2}+x\right)^{10}}{\left(\sqrt{1+x^2}-x\right)^{9}}dx=\frac1m\left(\left(\sqrt{1+x^2}+x\right)^{n}\left(n\sqrt{1+x^2}-x\right)\right)+C$, where $C$ is the constant of integration and $m,n\in\mathbb N$, then $m+n$ is equal to ___________.
questions.key_idea: Since $(\sqrt{1+x^2}+x)(\sqrt{1+x^2}-x)=1$, the integrand is $\left(\sqrt{1+x^2}+x\right)^{19}$; put $z=\sqrt{1+x^2}+x$ after $x=\tan\theta$.

alternate_solutions.idea: Put $x=\sinh u$: then $\sqrt{1+x^2}\pm x=e^{\pm u}$ and the integrand collapses to $e^{19u}\cosh u$.
solution: So the integral is $\frac{1}{360}z^{19}\left(19\sqrt{1+x^2}-x\right)+c$; $m=360$, $n=19$, $m+n=379$. Same answer.

useful_results: $\left(\sqrt{1+x^2}+x\right)\left(\sqrt{1+x^2}-x\right)=1$: reciprocal pair, so $\left(\sqrt{1+x^2}-x\right)^{-9}=\left(\sqrt{1+x^2}+x\right)^{9}$ and the integrand is $\left(\sqrt{1+x^2}+x\right)^{19}$.
With $x=\sinh u$: $\int\left(\sqrt{1+x^2}+x\right)^{k}dx=\int e^{ku}\cosh u\,du=\frac12\left[\frac{e^{(k+1)u}}{k+1}+\frac{e^{(k-1)u}}{k-1}\right]$ for $k\ne\pm1$.
Similarly $\int\left(x+\sqrt{x^2-1}\right)^kdx$ uses $x=\cosh u$ and $\int\left(\sqrt{a^2+x^2}+x\right)^kdx$ uses $x=a\sinh u$.
Check: for $F=\frac1{360}z^{19}\left(19\sqrt{1+x^2}-x\right)$ at $x=0$ ($z=1$, $z'=1$): $F'(0)=\frac1{360}(19\cdot19-1)=1$, the value of the integrand at $x=0$.

questions.question: If $\int\left(\frac1x+\frac1{x^3}\right)\left(\sqrt[23]{3x^{-24}+x^{-26}}\right)dx=-\frac{\alpha}{3(\alpha+1)}\left(3x^\beta+x^\gamma\right)^{\frac{\alpha+1}{\alpha}}+C$, $x>0$, $(\alpha,\beta,\gamma\in\mathbb Z)$, where $C$ is the constant of integration, then $\alpha+\beta+\gamma$ is equal to ___________.
questions.key_idea: Pull one factor $x^{-1}$ out of the root so the integrand is $\left(x^{-2}+x^{-4}\right)\left(3x^{-1}+x^{-3}\right)^{1/23}$, and put $t=3x^{-1}+x^{-3}$.
useful_results: $\int f'(x)\,[f(x)]^{p}dx=\frac{[f(x)]^{p+1}}{p+1}+C$: look for the inner function $f$ whose derivative appears as the other factor (here $f=3x^{-1}+x^{-3}$, $f'=-3(x^{-2}+x^{-4})$).
Factor out the common power under a root to expose $f$: $(3x^{-24}+x^{-26})=x^{-23}\,(3x^{-1}+x^{-3})$.
For $\int(a+bx^{-m})^{p}x^{-m-1}dx$-type integrals, the substitution $t=a+bx^{-m}$ works; the exponent $1/23$ plays no role beyond the power rule.
Check: the answer's exponent $\frac{\alpha+1}{\alpha}=\frac{24}{23}=1+\frac1{23}$, consistent with $p+1$ for $p=\frac1{23}$.

questions.question: If $\int\frac{2x^2+5x+9}{\sqrt{x^2+x+1}}dx=x\sqrt{x^2+x+1}+\alpha\sqrt{x^2+x+1}+\beta\log_e\left|x+\frac12+\sqrt{x^2+x+1}\right|+C$, where $C$ is the constant of integration, then $\alpha+2\beta$ is equal to ___________.
questions.key_idea: Differentiate both sides: the derivative of the right side over the common denominator $2\sqrt{x^2+x+1}$ must have numerator $2(2x^2+5x+9)$.
solution: Differentiate both sides with respect to $x$. Let $s=\sqrt{x^2+x+1}$, so $s'=\frac{2x+1}{2s}$.

alternate_solutions.idea: Complete the square, $x+\frac12=s$, and use the three standard integrals $\int\frac{s^2}{\sqrt{s^2+k}},\int\frac{s}{\sqrt{s^2+k}},\int\frac{1}{\sqrt{s^2+k}}$.

useful_results: $\int\frac{P_2(x)}{\sqrt{ax^2+bx+c}}dx=(px+q)\sqrt{ax^2+bx+c}+\lambda\int\frac{dx}{\sqrt{ax^2+bx+c}}$: differentiate both sides to find $p,q,\lambda$.

$\int\frac{dx}{\sqrt{x^2+x+1}}=\ln\left|x+\frac12+\sqrt{x^2+x+1}\right|+C$, and $\frac{d}{dx}\ln\left|x+\frac12+s\right|=\frac1s$ (general: $\frac{d}{dx}\ln\left|x+\sqrt{x^2+k}\right|=\frac1{\sqrt{x^2+k}}$).
For a degree-$n$ numerator over $\sqrt{\text{quadratic}}$ the ansatz is (polynomial of degree $n-1$)$\cdot\sqrt{\cdot}+\lambda\int\frac{dx}{\sqrt{\cdot}}$.
Check at $x=0$ ($s=1$, $s'=\frac12$): derivative of the right side $=s+xs'+\alpha s'+\frac\beta s=1+0+\frac74+\frac{25}4=9$, the integrand at $x=0$.

questions.question: If $\int\csc^5x\,dx=\alpha\cot x\csc x\left(\csc^2x+\frac32\right)+\beta\log_e\left|\tan\frac x2\right|+C$ where $\alpha,\beta\in\mathbb R$ and $C$ is the constant of integration, then the value of $8(\alpha+\beta)$ equals ___________.
questions.key_idea: Integrate $\csc^3x\cdot\csc^2x$ by parts (with $\int\csc^2x=-\cot x$) and use $\cot^2x=\csc^2x-1$ to get a reduction formula.
solution: Let $I=\int\csc^3x\cdot\csc^2x\,dx$. By parts, taking $\csc^3x$ as the first function and $\csc^2x$ as the second.
Let $I_1=\int\csc^3x\,dx=-\csc x\cot x-\int\cot^2x\csc x\,dx=-\csc x\cot x-\int\left(\csc^2x-1\right)\csc x\,dx$.
$I_1=-\csc x\cot x-I_1+\int\csc x\,dx$, so $2I_1=-\csc x\cot x+\ln\left|\tan\frac x2\right|$ and $I_1=-\frac12\csc x\cot x+\frac12\ln\left|\tan\frac x2\right|$.
From step 4: $4I=-\cot x\csc^3x+3I_1=-\cot x\csc^3x-\frac32\csc x\cot x+\frac32\ln\left|\tan\frac x2\right|+4c$.
questions.correction_note: PDF's second line reads I = -cot x cosec^3 x - 3I - 3 integral(cosec^3 x (cosec^2 x - 1)) dx, which counts the -3I term twice (the integral -3 int cosec^3(cosec^2-1) already equals -3I + 3 int cosec^3). The next line, I = -cot x cosec^3 x - 3I + 3 int cosec^3 x dx, and all later working and the answer 1 are correct. Extra '-3I' removed.

alternate_solutions.idea: Use the standard reduction formula $\int\csc^nx\,dx=-\frac{\csc^{n-2}x\cot x}{n-1}+\frac{n-2}{n-1}\int\csc^{n-2}x\,dx$ twice.
solution: For $n=3$: $\int\csc^3x\,dx=-\frac{\csc x\cot x}2+\frac12\int\csc x\,dx=-\frac{\csc x\cot x}{2}+\frac12\ln\left|\tan\frac x2\right|$.

useful_results: Reduction: $\int\csc^nx\,dx=-\frac{\csc^{n-2}x\cot x}{n-1}+\frac{n-2}{n-1}\int\csc^{n-2}x\,dx$, and the same with $\sec$: $\int\sec^nx\,dx=\frac{\sec^{n-2}x\tan x}{n-1}+\frac{n-2}{n-1}\int\sec^{n-2}x\,dx$.
Base cases: $\int\csc x\,dx=\ln\left|\tan\frac x2\right|+C$, $\int\csc^2x\,dx=-\cot x+C$, $\int\sec x\,dx=\ln|\sec x+\tan x|+C$.
For odd $n$ a log term appears; for even $n$ the result is a polynomial in $\cot x$ (or $\tan x$).
Check: $\frac{d}{dx}\left[-\frac14\csc x\cot x\left(\csc^2x+\frac32\right)+\frac38\ln\tan\frac x2\right]$ at $x=\frac\pi2$ is $\csc^5\frac\pi2=1$ (numerically verified).

questions.question: Let $I(x)=\int\sqrt{\frac{x+7}{x}}\,dx$ and $I(9)=12+7\log_e7$. If $I(1)=\alpha+7\log_e\left(1+2\sqrt2\right)$, then $\alpha^4$ is equal to ___________.
questions.key_idea: Write $\sqrt{\frac{x+7}x}=\frac{\sqrt{x+7}}{\sqrt x}$ and put $\sqrt x=t$ to reach $2\int\sqrt{t^2+7}\,dt$, a standard integral.
solution: Let $\sqrt x=t$; then $\frac1{2\sqrt x}dx=dt$, i.e. $\frac{dx}{\sqrt x}=2\,dt$.

alternate_solutions.idea: Rationalise to $\frac{x+7}{\sqrt{x^2+7x}}$, split off the derivative of the radicand, and use $\int\frac{dx}{\sqrt{x^2+7x}}$.

useful_results: $\int\sqrt{t^2+a^2}\,dt=\frac t2\sqrt{t^2+a^2}+\frac{a^2}2\ln\left(t+\sqrt{t^2+a^2}\right)+C$.
$\int\sqrt{\frac{x+a}{x}}dx=\sqrt{x(x+a)}+a\ln\left(\sqrt x+\sqrt{x+a}\right)+C$ for $x>0$, $a>0$; here $a=7$.
Different routes give antiderivatives that differ by a constant (here $\frac72\ln 2$ in the alternate form), so always fix $C$ using the given value in the same form.
Check: $\frac{d}{dx}\left[\sqrt{x(x+7)}+7\ln(\sqrt x+\sqrt{x+7})\right]$ at $x=1$ is $\frac{9}{2\sqrt8}+\frac{7}{2\sqrt8}=\frac{16}{2\sqrt8}=\sqrt8$, and $\sqrt{\frac{8}{1}}=\sqrt8$.

concepts: Constant of integration from a limit at $x=0$
questions.question: Let $f(x)=\int\frac{dx}{\left(3+4x^2\right)\sqrt{4-3x^2}}$, $|x|<\frac2{\sqrt3}$. If $f(0)=0$ and $f(1)=\frac1{\alpha\beta}\tan^{-1}\left(\frac\alpha\beta\right)$, $\alpha,\beta>0$, then $\alpha^2+\beta^2$ is equal to ___________.
questions.key_idea: Put $x=\frac1t$, then $4t^2-3=p^2$: the integral becomes $-\int\frac{dp}{3p^2+25}$, an arctangent.
solution: $f$ is continuous at $0$, so use $f(0)=\lim_{x\to0^+}f(x)$: $p\to\infty$ and $0=-\frac1{5\sqrt3}\cdot\frac\pi2+C$, so $C=\frac{\pi}{10\sqrt3}$.

alternate_solutions.idea: Put $u=\frac{x}{\sqrt{4-3x^2}}$: then $\frac{dx}{(4-3x^2)^{3/2}}=\frac{du}{4}$ and the integral is $\int\frac{du}{3+25u^2}$, with $f(0)=0$ at $u=0$ and no limit needed.

useful_results: For $\int\frac{dx}{(a+bx^2)\sqrt{c-dx^2}}$ put $u=\frac{x}{\sqrt{c-dx^2}}$ (or $x=\frac1t$): the radical disappears and the integral becomes $\int\frac{du}{A+Bu^2}$. Here $\frac{du}{dx}=\frac{c}{(c-dx^2)^{3/2}}$.
$\frac{d}{dx}\frac{x}{\sqrt{c-dx^2}}=\frac{c}{(c-dx^2)^{3/2}}$ is the key derivative; compare $\frac{d}{dx}\frac{x}{\sqrt{1-x^2}}=\frac1{(1-x^2)^{3/2}}$.
The antiderivative here is odd in $x$ ($\frac{1}{5\sqrt3}\tan^{-1}\frac{5x}{\sqrt3\sqrt{4-3x^2}}$), so $f(0)=0$ is automatic for it; a formula valid only for $x>0$ needs the limit $x\to0^+$.
$\tan^{-1}a+\cot^{-1}a=\frac\pi2$ and $\cot^{-1}a=\tan^{-1}\frac1a$ for $a>0$; used to rewrite the answer in the required form.
